newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya denies allegations of human rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Kenya denies allegations of human rights abuses.

text.p: Kenya on Thursday strongly rejected charges of human rights abuses made by Amnesty International ranging from police brutality to unfair trials.

Vice President George Saitoti also told Pierre Sane, Secretary-General of the London-based human rights watchdog, that Kenya did not plan meaningful constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections later this year.

Saitoti's meeting with Sane followed a memorandum by Amnesty that demanded a repeal of laws it described as unjust, spoke of torture of suspects and extra-judicial killings, and alleged interference in the judiciary by the executive.
On Tuesday, an independent report into the Kenyan legal system recommended sweeping changes after discovering widespread corruption and human rights abuses.

William Goodhart, one of the authors of the International Bar Association (IBA) report, told a news conference in London that its primary concerns were the independence of the judiciary in Kenya and the harassment of lawyers.
"The justice system is thought to lack independence," he said. "There is a widespread belief that many of the judges are willing to take a pro-government line."

Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi on Wednesday warned opposition politicians not to break the law in the runup to elections after police broke up a banned opposition rally called to press for constitutional reforms last weekend.
Saitoti said that while Kenya accepted and acted on fair and constructive criticism, it was upset by Amnesty's style.

"Government will not submit to recommendations which question our national sovereignty or are couched in the peremptory and prescriptive terms which are usually employed in master-servant relationship," said a government statement.
"Government hopes Amnesty will in future be sensitive to our national sovereignty and its recommendations will be couched in befitting language," added the statement, read by Saitoti.
Saitoti repeated Moi's pledge last weekend to repeal the unpopular Public Order Act but gave no details. He said other so-called unjust laws would have to wait until after elections.

He said Kenya was aware of its shortcomings with regard to reporting obligations under international treaties. But he saw the problem as inadequacy in technical expertise and lack of proper coordination which was now being addressed.
Saitoti said Kenya had outlawed torture, inquests were held in cases of death under police custody, the judiciary was free from interference by the executive and all trials were fair.

But he said that caning and the death penalty were controversial issues worldwide and a task force was still examining such cases in Kenya. He added that task force views were likely to be presented to parliament after elections.
On Wednesday, Sane expressed shock about Kenya's prisons.
He said that although there were 700 convicts on death row, there was no need for carrying out the death sentences because torture, disease and inhumane treatment killed them anyway.
The IBA revisited the trial of radical politician and government opponent Koigi wa Wamwere who was jailed in 1995 for robbery and who Amnesty called a prisoner of conscience.
IBA described his 18-month trial as the most serious abuse of the criminal process in Kenya in recent years. Koigi was freed on bail last December pending the hearing of his appeal.
